title: The narrow gate (Matthew 7:13–14)
hookLine: the way to life is narrow, and few find it

lines: A SMALL DOOR IN A WALL.
cards: A stadium is letting out. Thousands of people, all pouring toward the big main gates, the wide ramps, the parking lots. It's easy.
You don't even have to decide; the crowd carries you. Off to one side, there's a small door in a wall. You'd have to step out of the flow to find it.
You might have to turn sideways to get through. Nobody's holding it open. Jesus, near the end of his sermon, draws exactly that picture: two gates, two roads, and a crowd.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat." Notice the spelling: strait, s-t-r-a-i-t.

Not straight, like a ruler. Strait means narrow, tight, like the Strait of Gibraltar, a narrow stretch of sea. Some say the phrase the straight and narrow grew out of this verse, with strait heard as straight.
The Greek word is stenē: narrow, cramped.
Then verse fourteen: "Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it."

The word narrow there is even more vivid: pressed, squeezed, the way a crowd presses on you. It shares a root with the Greek word for trouble or hardship. So the road to life isn't described as pleasant.
It's a squeeze. What makes it narrow? The sermon itself: love your enemies, give in secret, don't judge, don't worry, do to others what you'd want.
None of that is complicated. All of it is hard. Christians read the few who find it in more than one way.
Some hear a sober warning about salvation. Others hear a description of discipleship: the way of the sermon is uncommon, and the crowd often goes the other direction.
Both readings agree on this: you don't drift through a narrow gate.
You have to choose it, one step out of the flow.

how: Some Christians hear this passage as a call to deliberate, daily choices that go against the easy way, and some churches use it in preaching about discipleship and conversion.

games.q: the crowd is heading for the wide gate. there's a small door off to one side. what does Jesus say?
o: follow the crowd; it knows the way.
games.why: "Enter ye in at the strait gate." the wide gate is easy; the narrow one has to be chosen.

practice: Think of one choice waiting for you today, with an easy way and a harder right way: the apology you've been putting off, the honest answer instead of the smooth one, the call you keep not making. Don't solve it yet.
Just picture the two gates, the wide one you'd slide through without thinking and the narrow one, and see yourself stepping sideways toward it.
